lead: An image forms in two separate steps. Geometry decides where a scene point lands on the sensor: a point at camera position (X, Y, Z) maps near (f X/Z, f Y/Z). Photometry decides how bright that pixel becomes: scene radiance passes through the lens, becomes irradiance on the sensor, and is converted to a number. Phone cameras, CCTV and ball-tracking in cricket depend on both. Keep the two models apart and most image-formation problems become simple. Some syllabi call the combined topic image formation.
prereq: You need: 1.4 for how light becomes a signal, and 1.2 for where acquisition sits in the system chain.

blocks.text: World coordinates (X<sub>w</sub>, Y<sub>w</sub>, Z<sub>w</sub>) fix the scene. Camera coordinates (X, Y, Z) are the same point after rotation and translation; this chapter uses only camera coordinates. Finding that rotation and translation is camera calibration, in Unit 5. Image coordinates (x, y) are distances on the sensor, in metres, before pixels.
Put the camera at the origin with its Z axis forward. A scene point has Z > 0. The image plane sits at distance f from the pinhole, where f is the focal length in metres. Pinhole projection is:
x = f X/Z,   y = f Y/Z
blocks.where: x and y are image-plane coordinates from the principal point; f is focal length in metres; X, Y, Z are camera coordinates in metres; Z is depth. Use magnitudes if your image plane is drawn behind the pinhole.

blocks.text: A point twice as far has half the image displacement. A real lens adds focus. The thin-lens equation is:

blocks.where: f is focal length; u is object distance from the lens; v is image distance from the lens. Use the same unit for all three. For a real object and real image, v > 0.

blocks.text: Magnification is m = -v/u. A negative m means an inverted image; size uses |m|. For sensor width w, field of view is θ = 2 arctan(w/(2f)). Depth of field is the range of u that stays acceptably sharp; a smaller aperture and shorter f enlarge it.

sections.h3: Photometry: how bright the pixel becomes

blocks.text: Radiance L is power per unit area per unit solid angle leaving a surface, in W/(m²·sr). Irradiance E is power per unit area falling on a surface, in W/m². The lens collects radiance and delivers irradiance to the sensor. A usable proportionality is E ∝ L (d/f)², where d is aperture diameter; the missing constant is not needed here.

Reflectance ρ is the fraction of incident irradiance reflected, 0 ≤ ρ ≤ 1. A Lambertian surface has the same radiance in every direction. Its outgoing radiance is L<sub>o</sub> = (ρ/π) E<sub>i</sub>. The BRDF is the general function for this; for a Lambertian surface it is ρ/π. Only a few syllabi go deeper.

Shading comes from geometry. If light arrives at angle θ to the surface normal, Ei = E0 cos θ. Then Lo = (ρ/π) E0 cos θ. This cosine law makes a sphere bright near the light and dark at the edge. The sensor converts irradiance to charge over exposure time t: pixel value = g E t + offset, then clipped and quantized. Quantization is in 1.6.

Geometry says where; photometry says how bright. In the worked example, geometry puts a 20 mm object at 500 mm from a 50 mm lens as an inverted 2.22 mm image. Photometry sets the pixel values on that image.

A pinhole has infinite depth of field and no focus, but collects little light. A lens collects more and focuses one distance; other distances blur. Field of view depends on sensor size and focal length, not object distance. Depth of field depends on aperture, focal length and distance.

spec.title: Geometry and photometry
spec.aria: Scene radiance is collected by a lens, becomes irradiance on the sensor, and is converted to a pixel value, separating photometry from geometry.

examples.question: A thin lens has focal length f = 50 mm. An object 20 mm high stands on the axis at object distance u = 500 mm. Find image distance v, magnification m, and image height h<sub>i</sub>. State whether the image is inverted.
steps: Magnification: m = -v/u = -55.56/500 = -0.111. The negative sign means the image is inverted.
Image height: h<sub>i</sub> = m h<sub>o</sub> = -0.111 × 20 mm = -2.22 mm. Size is 2.22 mm.
examples.answer: v = 55.56 mm, m = -0.111, and the image is 2.22 mm high and inverted.
examples.check:
f = 50
u = 500
h = 20
v = 1/(1/f - 1/u)
m = -v/u
hi = abs(m)*h
print(round(v, 2))
print(round(m, 3))
print(round(hi, 2))

traps: Pinhole projection has no focus. It gives infinite depth of field. Do not use 1/f = 1/u + 1/v for a pinhole question unless a lens is named.
Magnification sign: m = -v/u for a single thin lens. A negative m means inverted, not smaller. Use |m| for size.
Units: f, u and v must be in the same unit. Mixing 50 mm with 0.5 m gives a wrong v by 1000 times.
Radiance L and irradiance E are not interchangeable. L is per unit solid angle; E is per unit area. The sensor receives irradiance.
Field of view depends on sensor size and focal length, not object distance. Depth of field depends on aperture, focal length and distance.

quiz.q: Define radiance and irradiance, with units.
quiz.a: Radiance L is power per unit area per unit solid angle, in W/(m²·sr). Irradiance E is power per unit area, in W/m².

quiz.q: Why does a pinhole have infinite depth of field while a lens does not?
quiz.a: A pinhole passes one ray per scene point, so no blur circle forms at any distance. A lens focuses one object distance; other distances spread light into a blur circle, so sharpness is limited.

quiz.q: A thin lens has f = 25 mm and u = 300 mm. Find v.
A 50 mm lens is used at f/2 and then at f/8. Which setting gives larger depth of field, and what is the cost?
quiz.a: f/8 gives larger depth of field because the aperture is smaller, so blur circles grow more slowly away from focus. The cost is less light, so a longer exposure or higher gain is needed.

quiz.q: A sensor is 36 mm wide and the lens has f = 50 mm. Find the horizontal field of view.
What does a Lambertian surface assume, and what is its BRDF?
quiz.a: It assumes outgoing radiance is the same in every direction. Its BRDF is ρ/π, where ρ is reflectance.

quiz.q: In the worked example, the object moves from u = 500 mm to u = 1000 mm. Find v and the new image height for the same 20 mm object and f = 50 mm.
quiz.a: 1/v = 1/50 - 1/1000 = 19/1000 mm⁻¹, so v = 52.63 mm. m = -52.63/1000 = -0.0526, so image height is 1.05 mm. The image is smaller and closer to the focal point.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, image formation models sit inside camera pipelines, auto-exposure and HDR. Research extends the Lambertian model to measured BRDFs and physics-based rendering. Search next for thin-lens depth of field, radiometry radiance irradiance, and Lambertian BRDF.
